metadata.title: X-Guard Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master X-Guard Bottom position in BJJ. Comprehensive guide covering sweeps, entries, and retention. Powerful off-balancing position with 65% sweep success rate at advanced level.

overview:
X-Guard Bottom is a powerful open guard position where the bottom practitioner controls the opponent using their legs in an 'X' configuration around one of the opponent's legs. The position is characterized by one leg hooking behind the opponent's knee while the other controls the hip or belt line, creating a crossing pattern that gives the position its name. This configuration provides exceptional off-balancing control and sweep opportunities.

The X-Guard emerged as a revolutionary position in modern BJJ, popularized by Marcelo Garcia who demonstrated its effectiveness at the highest levels of competition. The position offers a systematic approach to dealing with standing opponents and is particularly effective against knee slice passes and other pressure-based attacks. Unlike traditional guards, X-Guard creates mechanical advantages through leg control rather than grips, making it highly effective in both gi and no-gi contexts.

From a strategic standpoint, X-Guard Bottom serves as both a sweeping platform and a transitional hub to other leg entanglement positions. The position's power comes from controlling the opponent's base while simultaneously threatening multiple sweeping directions. Advanced practitioners use X-Guard as part of an integrated guard system, flowing seamlessly between Single Leg X, Reverse X-Guard, and Deep Half variations based on opponent reactions.
state_invariants: Bottom practitioner's inside leg (closer to opponent's centerline) hooks deeply behind opponent's near knee, with the foot positioned past the knee joint to prevent escape and create off-balancing leverage through hamstring pressure

Bottom practitioner's outside leg extends across opponent's hip or belt line, with the foot or shin creating a barrier that controls distance and prevents forward pressure while maintaining the crossing 'X' configuration

Opponent is standing or in combat base with one leg isolated and controlled by the X-Guard configuration, while their other leg remains free but unable to effectively generate base or forward pressure
Bottom practitioner's upper body is positioned perpendicular to opponent's trapped leg, with shoulders on the mat and hips elevated off the ground to maintain active tension in the leg configuration
Bottom practitioner maintains hand control on opponent's trapped leg ankle or pants, or controls the free leg to prevent opponent from establishing stable base
prerequisites: Opponent is standing or in combat base position
Bottom practitioner has isolated one of opponent's legs
Bottom practitioner's inside leg has access to hook behind opponent's knee
Bottom practitioner has sufficient space to configure legs in X-pattern
Opponent's weight is distributed such that the trapped leg can be off-balanced
key_principles: Maintain deep knee hook with inside leg to control opponent's base and create off-balancing leverage
Keep outside leg active and extended across opponent's hip to control distance and prevent forward pressure
Elevate hips off the mat to create tension in the X-configuration and maintain active control
Use upper body positioning perpendicular to opponent's trapped leg to maximize sweeping angles
Control opponent's ankle or pants with hands to prevent them from stepping over or escaping the position
Threaten multiple sweeping directions simultaneously to create defensive dilemmas for opponent
Transition seamlessly between X-Guard variations (Single Leg X, Reverse X) based on opponent's reactions

Opponent sits back to break X-Guard configuration
Opponent attempts to step over the outside leg
Opponent drives knee forward through X-Guard

decision_tree.condition: If opponent maintains strong upright posture with both feet planted and good base
If opponent attempts to backstep or circle away from the X-Guard configuration
If opponent sits back to break X-Guard or attempts to smash forward with knee pressure
If opponent attempts to step over the outside leg while trapped leg remains controlled

common_errors.error: Allowing hips to remain flat on the mat instead of elevating them
common_errors.consequence: Loss of tension in the X-Guard configuration, making sweeps ineffective and allowing opponent to establish pressure and pass
common_errors.correction: Actively bridge hips off the mat to create upward pressure through the inside leg hook and maintain tight X-configuration with constant tension

common_errors.error: Hooking too shallow behind opponent's knee with inside leg
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily extract their leg by stepping back, breaking the X-Guard and transitioning to a dominant passing position
common_errors.correction: Drive inside leg deep past opponent's knee joint until foot clears the back of the knee, creating a secure hook that prevents backward extraction

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's ankle or pants with hands
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can freely step over or reposition their legs, defeating the X-Guard's off-balancing mechanics and establishing dominant passing grips
common_errors.correction: Maintain consistent grip on opponent's trapped leg ankle or pants while using free hand to control their free leg or establish grips for sweeping mechanics

common_errors.error: Positioning upper body parallel to opponent's trapped leg instead of perpendicular
common_errors.consequence: Reduced sweeping angles and leverage, making it difficult to off-balance opponent and complete sweeps effectively
common_errors.correction: Align shoulders perpendicular to opponent's trapped leg with upper body forming a 'T' shape, maximizing sweeping leverage and creating multiple directional threats

common_errors.error: Keeping outside leg passive or bent instead of actively extended
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can drive forward pressure through the gap, smashing the X-Guard and advancing to passing positions like knee slice or leg drag
common_errors.correction: Maintain active extension with outside leg across opponent's hip, creating a rigid barrier that controls distance and prevents forward pressure

common_errors.error: Failing to transition when opponent begins to escape or counter the X-Guard
common_errors.consequence: Getting stuck in a defensive position as opponent establishes passing control, leading to guard pass and loss of the position
common_errors.correction: Proactively transition to Single Leg X, Ashi Garami, or Deep Half based on opponent's escape direction, maintaining control through positional flow

training_drills.name: X-Guard Entry and Sweep Repetitions
training_drills.description: Partner stands in combat base while you practice entering X-Guard from seated guard or butterfly. Focus on deep knee hook, hip elevation, and completing sweeps to mount or top position. Perform 10 repetitions per side, emphasizing smooth entry mechanics and explosive sweep execution.

training_drills.name: X-Guard Retention Against Pressure
training_drills.description: Partner attempts to pass using knee slice, stack, or backstep escapes while you maintain X-Guard configuration and counter their attempts. Focus on transitioning between X-Guard variations (Single Leg X, Reverse X) to retain guard. Partner gradually increases resistance over 3-minute rounds.

training_drills.name: X-Guard Positional Sparring
training_drills.description: Start in established X-Guard Bottom position. Your goal is to sweep or submit; opponent's goal is to pass guard. Reset to X-Guard after each successful action. This builds timing, decision-making, and transition skills under realistic pressure.

training_drills.name: X-Guard to Leg Entanglement Flow Drill
training_drills.description: Practice flowing from X-Guard to Single Leg X to Ashi Garami and back based on partner's movements. Partner provides graduated resistance, moving in different directions to simulate escape attempts. Focus on maintaining leg control throughout transitions.

expert_insights.danaher: X-Guard represents a paradigm shift in guard theory, moving away from grip-based control to mechanical leg-based control systems. The position's effectiveness stems from its ability to simultaneously destroy the opponent's base while creating multiple directional sweeping threats. The inside leg hook functions as a powerful lever that controls the opponent's hamstring and knee joint, while the outside leg creates a rigid barrier that prevents forward pressure. The key to mastering X-Guard lies in understanding that it is not a static position but rather a dynamic control system that flows between variations based on opponent reactions. Advanced practitioners develop the ability to maintain the essential mechanical properties of X-Guard - base destruction and directional threat - while transitioning seamlessly between X-Guard, Single Leg X, and leg entanglement positions. The position requires precise hip elevation and active leg tension to maintain control; passive execution leads to immediate failure as the opponent can simply pressure through the position.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: X-Guard is one of the most high-percentage sweeping positions in modern competition BJJ, particularly effective against standing opponents who are trying to establish distance for knee slice or toreando passes. In my competition experience, X-Guard serves as both an attacking platform and a transitional hub to leg entanglements, which is where the real finishing opportunities emerge. The key to making X-Guard work at the elite level is developing ruthless efficiency in your entries - you need to establish the position immediately and sweep before the opponent can set their defense. I particularly favor using X-Guard as a transitional position to Single Leg X and Ashi Garami, where the submission opportunities are far more abundant. The most common mistake I see is practitioners trying to hold X-Guard statically rather than flowing through it as part of a larger guard system. Against world-class opponents, you have a very narrow window to sweep from X-Guard before they start their pass, so your timing and explosive execution must be perfect. The position is especially powerful in no-gi where grip fighting is less of a factor and pure mechanical control dominates.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: X-Guard is a fundamental position in the 10th Planet system, and we've developed numerous creative entries and variations that work exceptionally well in no-gi contexts. The beauty of X-Guard is that it doesn't rely on gi grips, making it equally effective whether you're wearing a gi or not. We emphasize using X-Guard as an entry point to our leg lock game, particularly flowing to Honey Hole and saddle positions for heel hook attacks. The traditional X-Guard sweep is great, but we've found even more success using it as a transitional position that keeps opponents guessing and off-balance. One of our key innovations is combining X-Guard with rubber guard concepts, using the trapped leg control to set up unique submission opportunities. We also drill extensively on maintaining X-Guard against modern passing methods like the knee slice and leg drag, developing specific counter-reactions that flow into either sweeps or leg entanglements. The position requires constant movement and adjustment - you can't just sit there and hold it statically. The key is building a systematic understanding of where to go based on how the opponent reacts, turning X-Guard into a hub position that connects to multiple offensive pathways.

metadata.title: X-Guard | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master X-Guard in BJJ. Complete guide covering setup, control, sweeps, and transitions. Advanced guard with 70% sweep success rate at high levels.

overview: X-Guard is an advanced open guard variation where the bottom player entangles one of the opponent's legs using both of their own legs in an "X" formation, creating powerful leverage for sweeps and transitions. This position provides exceptional control over the opponent's balance and mobility by eliminating one of their posting bases while creating strong elevating forces. X-Guard serves as a critical junction point between traditional sweeping guards and modern leg entanglement systems, offering both offensive sweep opportunities and pathways to ashi garami positions. The position is characterized by the top leg hooking around the outside of the opponent's leg while the bottom leg hooks inside, with upper body grips controlling posture and preventing counter-balancing. Developed and popularized by Marcelo Garcia, X-Guard has become a fundamental component of modern BJJ guard systems, particularly in no-gi competition where it offers high-percentage sweeps against standing opponents.
state_invariants: One of opponent's legs is controlled between both of your legs, with your top leg wrapping around the outside of their thigh and your bottom leg hooking inside their knee or ankle, creating the characteristic X formation that traps their posting leg

Your hips are positioned directly underneath the opponent's center of gravity with your shoulders angled approximately 45 degrees to their centerline, allowing you to generate upward lifting force through leg extension while maintaining mobility

Upper body connection is maintained through grips on the opponent's opposite leg (pants or ankle), belt, or upper body (collar or sleeve in gi), preventing them from establishing stable posture or creating distance to escape the leg entanglement

The opponent is forced into a compromised standing or semi-standing position with only one leg available for base, making them vulnerable to directional sweeps and unable to effectively pass or establish strong top pressure
prerequisites: Hip mobility and hamstring flexibility to maintain leg positioning
Understanding of leverage mechanics and fulcrum principles
Basic sweeping concepts including off-balancing and timing
Familiarity with leg positioning control and hook maintenance
Ability to create and maintain upper body connections under resistance
Competence in open guard retention fundamentals
key_principles: Control opponent's base leg through proper X formation with top leg around outside and bottom leg hooking inside
Maintain upper body connection through grips to prevent posture recovery and base establishment
Create and exploit leverage through extension and retraction of the legs in opposition
Manipulate opponent's weight distribution by elevating and angling your hips to compromise their balance
Prevent opponent from establishing secondary base or freeing their trapped leg through constant adjustment
Transition seamlessly between X-Guard variations (standard, reverse, single leg X) based on opponent's reactions
Generate sweeping power through hip elevation and directional control rather than muscular effort alone

If opponent sits back or drops weight to defend sweep

common_errors.error: Poor leg positioning with hooks too shallow or legs crossed incorrectly
common_errors.consequence: Opponent easily frees their trapped leg, escapes the position, and passes to side control or mount without resistance
common_errors.correction: Ensure top leg wraps deeply around outside of thigh while bottom leg hooks inside at knee level, creating tight X formation with constant tension toward your centerline

common_errors.error: Neglecting upper body connections and grips
common_errors.consequence: Opponent establishes strong upright posture, creates distance, and either passes around the legs or simply steps out of the entanglement
common_errors.correction: Maintain at least one strong grip (opposite ankle, belt, or collar) to control posture and prevent opponent from creating space or establishing balance

common_errors.error: Static positioning without active hip movement or adjustment
common_errors.consequence: Position becomes stagnant with no sweeping opportunities, allowing opponent to methodically work their way free or establish passing angles
common_errors.correction: Constantly adjust hip position and angle to stay underneath opponent's center of gravity, using small movements to maintain optimal leverage and create sweep angles

common_errors.error: Overextending legs too early before establishing proper control
common_errors.consequence: Loss of control over trapped leg, inability to generate sweeping power, and vulnerability to leg drag or knee slice passes
common_errors.correction: First secure the X formation with proper hooks and upper body connection, then progressively extend to create sweeping leverage only when fully established

common_errors.error: Premature sweep attempts without proper off-balancing setup
common_errors.consequence: Failed sweep attempts that waste energy, alert opponent to defensive needs, and create opportunities for them to counter-pass or establish dominant position
common_errors.correction: Use initial movements to compromise opponent's balance and force reactions, then execute sweep when they are already off-balance and unable to recover base

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to bring free leg back toward trapped leg to establish stable base
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates strong defensive structure with both legs together, neutralizing the sweeping mechanics and making position retention difficult
common_errors.correction: Use grips and hip positioning to control opponent's free leg, preventing them from bringing it close to the trapped leg and maintaining their compromised balance

expert_insights.danaher: X-Guard represents a critical junction point in the lower body control hierarchy, positioned between traditional sweeping guards and modern leg entanglement systems. The mechanical advantage stems from creating a fulcrum underneath the opponent's center of gravity while simultaneously removing one of their two posting bases, resulting in a 50% reduction in their base stability. The position's effectiveness relies on understanding that sweeping power comes not from muscular force but from precise angular positioning of your hips relative to their center of mass combined with controlled leg extension. Most practitioners fail to recognize that X-Guard functions as part of a larger system including Single Leg X, Reverse X, and standard ashi garami positions, with transitions between these variations occurring based on predictable defensive reactions. The key to mastery lies in viewing X-Guard not as a static position but as a dynamic control system where your constant adjustment maintains the opponent in a perpetually compromised state, unable to establish base or create effective passing angles.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: X-Guard is one of the highest percentage sweeping positions in modern competition, particularly effective against opponents who maintain upright posture in their passing game. In my competitive experience, the position offers three critical pathways: direct sweeps when the opponent remains standing, leg entanglement entries when they sit to defend, and technical stand-ups when they stall. The most important competitive adjustment I've made is recognizing when to abandon the traditional sweep in favor of the ashi garami transition, especially against leg lock-aware opponents who will immediately sit to defend. Against elite competition, X-Guard serves primarily as a transitional control position rather than a finishing position, with the goal being to force reactions that open up either the sweep or the leg entanglement. The position's competitive viability increased dramatically when practitioners began integrating it with Single Leg X and standard ashi positions, creating a system where the opponent cannot effectively defend all pathways simultaneously. My approach emphasizes using X-Guard to create binary decisions where both options lead to advantageous positions.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Within the 10th Planet system, X-Guard represents a critical gateway position that connects our upper body control systems with our leg lock game, though we've developed some unique variations from the standard approach. We emphasize using X-Guard with specific no-gi grips like the waist grip or underhook rather than traditional gi grips, which changes the sweeping mechanics significantly but increases transition speed to leg locks. One innovation we've integrated is combining X-Guard entries with our rubber guard and lockdown systems, creating unexpected pathways that opponents don't commonly train to defend. The position becomes particularly powerful when you understand it as part of a larger sequence starting from mission control or lockdown and flowing through X-Guard into either sweeps or our electric chair position. We also place heavy emphasis on the technical stand-up from X-Guard, which most traditional systems underutilize but which opens up entirely different game trees including our twister series from standing back control. The key adaptation for modern no-gi is accepting that X-Guard retention is less important than using it as a transition point to create chaos and force the opponent into unfamiliar territory where creativity wins.

metadata.title: X-Guard Top | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master X-Guard Top in BJJ. Control opponent's inverted guard with strategic base, pressure passing, and leg attack entries. 60-75% pass success rate across skill levels.

overview:
X-Guard Top represents the top player's position when facing an opponent in X-Guard, where the bottom player has established an inverted configuration with one leg hooking behind the knee and the other controlling the hip or torso. This is fundamentally a guard passing scenario where the top player must navigate the opponent's leverage-based control system. The primary challenge lies in maintaining balance and posture while systematically dismantling the bottom player's structural controls.

From the top position, success depends on understanding the mechanical disadvantages inherent to X-Guard - particularly the bottom player's vulnerability to forward pressure and their reliance on specific grips and hooks for positional maintenance. The top player enjoys significant advantages including gravity, the ability to generate downward pressure, and multiple passing pathways that exploit the inverted nature of the guard. Strategic options include direct pressure passing, leg entanglement counters, and explosive movements that overwhelm the bottom player's reactive capabilities.

This position is critical in modern BJJ competition, as X-Guard has become a fundamental component of many guard systems. Proficiency in dealing with X-Guard from the top perspective is essential for any serious competitor, particularly in no-gi contexts where the position appears frequently. Understanding both the defensive requirements and offensive opportunities from this position separates competent passers from elite ones.
state_invariants: Top player maintains upright or forward-leaning posture with base on at least one leg, while opponent lies on their side/back beneath with inverted leg configuration
Bottom player has established X-Guard structure with one leg hooking behind top player's knee (typically far leg) and other leg controlling hip, torso, or creating elevation
Top player's hips positioned above opponent's center of gravity, creating downward pressure potential and limiting bottom player's ability to generate upward sweeping force
Top player maintains balance through strategic weight distribution and grip fighting, preventing bottom player from destabilizing stance or creating sweep angles
One or both of top player's legs remains potentially entangled or controlled by bottom player's leg hooks, requiring careful extraction and base management
prerequisites: Opponent has successfully established X-Guard bottom position with hook behind knee
Top player has maintained standing or combat base posture rather than being swept
Bottom player has inverted their body underneath top player's base
Top player has at least one leg still weighted and providing base
Grips have been established or are being contested between both players
key_principles: Maintain forward pressure and low center of gravity to prevent opponent from creating elevation or sweep angles
Control distance by managing opponent's sleeve grips and preventing them from extending their arms to manipulate posture
Keep weight distributed strategically to prevent being swept while maintaining mobility for passing
Attack the bottom player's structural controls systematically - removing hooks before advancing position
Use crossface and shoulder pressure when possible to flatten opponent and reduce their mobility
Recognize leg entanglement opportunities as the opponent's legs are already engaged with yours
Maintain calm patience while systematically dismantling the guard rather than rushing into sweep attempts

common_errors.error: Standing fully upright with narrow base while opponent has established hooks
common_errors.consequence: Creates maximum leverage for opponent's sweep attempts and makes balance recovery difficult when opponent elevates
common_errors.correction: Maintain forward lean with wide base, keeping hips low and weight distributed to prevent opponent from generating effective sweeping angles

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to secure deep sleeve grips that control distance and posture
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can manipulate your upper body position, create angles for sweeps, and prevent forward pressure from being effective
common_errors.correction: Fight grips aggressively by stripping sleeves, establishing your own collar/head control, and maintaining proper distance management

common_errors.error: Attempting to pass before removing or controlling the far leg hook behind the knee
common_errors.consequence: The far hook provides opponent with primary sweeping mechanism and positional control that will prevent successful passing attempts
common_errors.correction: Systematically remove or redirect the far hook first using knee extraction, crossface pressure, or leg weave techniques before advancing

common_errors.error: Jumping or stepping over opponent's legs without proper weight distribution or timing
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can easily sweep you mid-transition or establish more dominant positions like back control or mount
common_errors.correction: Use controlled, pressured movements with proper base maintenance, passing only when opponent's structure is compromised

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control opponent's hips when their hooks begin to fail
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can re-establish guard, transition to other guards like butterfly or single leg X, or create scrambling opportunities
common_errors.correction: Immediately apply hip pressure and crossface control when hooks weaken, consolidating position before they can recover structure

common_errors.error: Ignoring leg entanglement opportunities when opponent inverts deeply
common_errors.consequence: Missing high-percentage finishing opportunities and allowing opponent to maintain control of the engagement
common_errors.correction: Recognize when opponent's inversion exposes them to saddle or ashi positions and capitalize on these submissions or dominant positions

expert_insights.danaher: X-Guard top position represents a fascinating study in leverage mechanics and systematic dismantling of opponent structure. The bottom player's inverted configuration creates specific mechanical disadvantages that the educated top player can exploit ruthlessly. The primary weakness lies in their reliance on the far leg hook - once this critical connection is severed or compromised, the entire position collapses. Your strategic focus should be threefold: first, establish dominant grips that prevent opponent extension and distance manipulation; second, apply forward pressure that compromises their ability to generate elevation; third, systematically remove the far hook through crossface pressure, knee extraction, or leg weaving. The beautiful aspect of this position is that opponent attempts to strengthen their position often expose them to leg entanglement attacks - particularly when they invert deeper seeking ashi garami positions. A competent top player should view X-Guard not as a threatening position to escape from, but rather as an opportunity to demonstrate superior understanding of positional mechanics and transition to dominant positions or leg attack systems.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: When I'm in X-Guard top, I'm hunting for the pass but I'm also extremely aware of the leg attack opportunities. Most competitors make the mistake of only thinking about passing - they miss that X-Guard bottom is actually a terrible position for the bottom guy if you understand leg locks. The moment they start inverting or trying to transition to their leg attack systems, that's when you counter and enter your own leg entanglement. I've finished countless matches from saddle entries against opponents who thought they were attacking from X-Guard. The key is pressure - constant, heavy forward pressure that makes them uncomfortable and forces mistakes. Don't let them play their game at their pace. Strip their grips, smash through their structure, and if they give you the saddle entry, take it immediately. In competition, I probably finish more matches from leg locks off of X-Guard counters than I do from passing to traditional positions. The position has become so popular that being elite at dealing with it from top is absolutely mandatory for high-level no-gi competition.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: X-Guard top is where you need to be ready for anything because the bottom guy can transition fast if you're not paying attention. At 10th Planet, we teach guys to recognize when the opponent is setting up their transitions and beat them to the punch. If they're going inverted trying to get to ashi or saddle, you should be entering your leg attack before they complete theirs - it's all about timing and recognition. The grip fighting is crucial here - you cannot let them control your sleeves and manipulate your posture. Once they have those grips, they can create angles and sweeps all day. I like the crossface smash pass from here because it takes away their mobility and forces them flat, which kills the X-Guard structure completely. But you've got to be fluid - if the smash isn't there, maybe you step over and take the back, or you weave through and establish headquarters. The worst thing you can do is be static and predictable. Keep them guessing, keep the pressure on, and don't be afraid to abandon one pass and switch to another if they're defending well. X-Guard is beatable if you stay mobile and aggressive.
